Amanda Scarpone Poland, Maine March 4, 2025
To Members of the Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee: Thank you for the opportunity to address the Committee. My name is Amanda Scarpone, I am a resident of Poland, Maine, and I am a public health professional who works in the non-profit and philanthropy field. I am also a Board member of the nonprofit organization Cultivating Community. I am writing to you today in support of LD 415, An Act to Support Hunger Prevention in Maine. As a public health professional, I know that equitable access to healthy food is a key part of Mainers having healthy and thriving lives. This bill would provide an additional $1million per year to the Statewide Hunger Relief Program, which is funding especially needed now as federal funding freezes put funding for these types of programs in jeopardy. This act is key for adequate nutrition in the state, and it provides a steady source of income for our own farmers in Maine. The programs enabled by this act also makes our communities more resilient and less dependent on the national food systems that are often unstable and also do not provide access to culturally important foods that our neighbors deserve. Maine is a state that prides itself on its fresh food, our farms, and our innovative restaurants. We should also pride ourselves on how we feed each other, and our communities. LD 415 helps us do just that. Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee. I urge you to vote "Ought to Pass" on LD415.
Thank you, Amanda Scarpone

Anna Markow Brunswick LD 415
Dear members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry.
My name is Anna Markow, I am a resident of Brunswick, and I am writing today as a farm worker and farmer's market customer to express my support of LD 468 - An Act to Address Food Insecurity by Helping Maine Residents Access Locally Produced Food.
Farmer's markets are frequently stereotyped as an upper class privilege, but our community of farmers believe that everyone deserves access to fresh, healthy local food, regardless of income. Those who have less should not be punished by denying access to the best possible quality food. I am delighted every single time I accept Harvest Bucks or any supplemental payment for our produce, because I know the food I work very hard to grow is getting to the people who need it most. I spent years of my life cooking in upscale restaurants where I myself could not afford to eat, and my transition to farming as a second career is driven by the urge to feed EVERYONE.

Good moming, Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of the
Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. I am Representative Annie
Graham and I represent House District 105, which includes North Yarmouth and most of Gray. I
am here today to present LD 415, An Act to Support Hunger Prevention in Maine.

This bill provides an additional $1M per year to the Statewide Hunger Relief Program,
administered by the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry. The Statewide
Hunger Relief Program currently provides $1M per year to Mainers Feeding Mainers, which is
administered by Good Shepherd Food Bank. This investment will bring the state's contribution
to $2M annually. Good Shepherd Food Bank currently spends an additional $2M of donor
dollars to support Mainers Feeding Mainers and will continue to dedicate donor dollars to the
program.

Mainers Feeding Mainers is a collaborative initiative by Good Shepherd Food Bank aimed at enhancing food security in Maine by sourcing fresh, locally produced food from Maine farmers and fishermen. This program provides nutritious food to those accessing community food
pantries and also supports local agricultural and fishing communities.

Directors of Piscataquis Regional Food Center (PRFC). Thank you for allowing me to speak with
you today. Piscataquis Regional Food Center serves one of the most rural and impoverished
counties in Maine. I am here today to speak in strong support of LD41 5 which would provide

Gillian Cridler Portland LD 415
I am writing as someone who works in food insecurity to support of LD 415, An Act to Support Hunger Prevention in Maine. Good Shepherd Food Bank's Mainers Feeding Mainers program addresses food insecurity, provides a reliable market for farmers, and connects Mainers to local agriculture.
Addressing hunger through local food is a compassionate way to provide a diverse array of nourishing foods to community members facing food insecurity. Local food helps to fortify the nutrition of the food that pantries are able to share with their communities. After a long winter, there is excitement for the return of fresh, local food. The Mainers Feeding Mainers program helps ensure that all Mainers have access to locally grown produce and can participate in the joy and nourishment of cooking with local food.
Maine farmers also benefit from the partnerships created by the Mainers Feeding Mainers program. Participating farmers are given a reliable market and a predictable income for their produce. This provides stability to a profession that is more susceptible to economic and climate variables. Farmers have the benefit of a dependable, direct market to consumers and consumers benefit by having access to nutritious local food and connection to local agriculture.
Strong, mutually beneficial partnerships between farmers, pantries and our food insecure communities are essential in making sure our local food system is resilient and accessible to all Mainers. I have seen first hand the nutritional impact that local food can have in the charitable food system. Likewise, I have also seen the impact that a steady, predicable market has on the livelihood of farmers. There are great relationships between pantries and farmers that are nurtured by this program. I hope you support LD 415 and continue to invest in the state of Maine's ability to grow food and feed food insecure communities. Thank you, Gillian Cridler

Narrative Summary of the Approach to Meeting Program Requirements
Good Shepherd Food Bank's Mainers Feeding Mainers (MFM) program was formed 15 years
ago with the dual purpose of supporting Maine's food production infrastructure, while also providing nutritious, fresh food to Maine's statewide emergency food distribution network. The program has grown and expanded to include 93 Maine farmers and food producers, and currently provides food to emergency relief organizations in all 16 counties of the state, totaling 600 emergency food distribution organizations.
Since its inception, MFM has expanded beyond getting local produce to food pantries. Through
collaborations with processors such as Pineland Dairy Farm, Oakhurst Dairy, Maine Coast Fishermen's Association, W.A. Bean and Maine Grains, cheese, milk, fish, flour, oats, bread and
meat products are now available for our network agencies. We also remain committed to
partnering with underserved farmers and producers especially BIPOC farmers. MFM works

market pricing changes, or the farm has product available to donate.

The MFM Program Manager meets with the farm partners during the winter and early spring to
establish written commitments in the form of flexible Letters of Understanding (LOU) with each
farm partner. These LOUs specify the products to be grown, estimated volumes and prices, and delivery methods. The Food Bank guarantees the total revenue stated in the LOU, unless
a farmer is unable to provide any product.
Throughout the growing season, the MFM Program Manager stays in regular contact with each
farmer. GSFB will amend the LOU's to meet the farmer's needs, if product availability or
market pricing changes, or the farm has product available to donate.
Farms invoice the Food Bank as product is transferred (either via delivery, pick-up, or partner delivery). The Food Bank pays these invoices typically within 15 days of invoice receipt. Farm-to-Pantry produce is delivered according to a schedule agreed upon between the farmer and the partner agency. Farm-to-Warehouse produce is made available to all network partners
via the GSFB online shopping portal. Regardless of distribution channel, all MFM produce is
provided at no cost to partners.

No child should have to worry about when their next meal will come, and yet, in Maine, we know that food insecurity remains a daily reality for far too many families. My own experiences balancing the responsibilities of parenthood and public service have deepened my commitment to policies that support working families, ensure access to basic needs, and strengthen our communities.

Hunger is not just a symptom of poverty--it is a structural issue that affects health, education, workforce participation, and long-term community prosperity. By investing in hunger prevention services, we are investing in stronger families, healthier children, and a more resilient Maine.
My district, home to hardworking fishermen, small business owners, and families that have lived on these islands for generations, is not immune to the challenges of food insecurity. With the rising costs of living, families in rural and coastal areas often find themselves stretched thin,

Dear Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry,
My name is Susanne Lee, and I am a Faculty Fellow at the Senator George J. Mitchell Center for Sustainability Solutions at the University of Maine. Since 2019, we have worked as part a multi-disciplinary faculty and student team focused on ending wasted food and food loss in our state. Our team works with key Maine food waste stakeholders - farms, businesses, schools, organizations, municipalities, and consumers throughout the state - to identify, develop, and test sustainable food loss & waste solutions that will equitably benefit all Maine people.
My colleagues include Prof. Travis Blackmer (Economics), Dr. Ivan Fernandez (Soil & Climate Science) and Dr. Jason Bolton (Food & Nutrition Sciences). Our expertise is also based on research and collaborations with leading national food waste organizations like ReFED, Zero Food Waste Coalition, Harvard Food Law & Policy, and the EPA's Food Too Good To Waste Network, as well as our own Maine food waste advisory group of over forty leading Maine food system stakeholders. In addition, our team works closely with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) using their Food Waste Hierarchy to guide the development of sustainable food loss and wasted food solutions for our state.
Today, I am submitting written testimony on behalf of R1 UMaine in support of LD 415, An Act to Support Hunger Prevention in Maine. This testimony has been informed by our University food loss and waste research and statewide outreach.
Based on our team's most recent work on the Maine Food Loss & Waste Generation Study 2024, Maine has an estimated 361,506 tons (723 million pounds) of wasted food and food loss annually. The economic cost to our state is great and is estimated at over $1.3 billion dollars annually, while the environmental impact is equivalent to the carbon footprint of 302,142 passenger vehicles annually - more than the number of passenger cars (295,849) registered in Maine in 2023.

Of that total, the Farms and Agriculture sector in Maine generates the largest amount of food loss estimated at over 90,000 tons annually - commonly caused by unharvested, unanticipated surplus products. This farm and agriculture food loss is not only the economic loss for our agriculture economy but also the loss of the valuable labor, energy, land, and the almost � of fresh water resources that are used to produce food that is never eaten. While the majority of this farm food loss is plowed under in the fields and not landfilled, the Study finds that "there is great potential to fight hunger by recovering this surplus and redistributing it to feed Mainers."
In addition, we are finalizing a current research study to examine the link between Maine's food loss and waste and our charitable food system entitled, Unlocking the Economic, Social, and Environmental Benefits of Using Surplus Food in Maine: A Qualitative Survey of the Challenges and Opportunities for Redistributing Maine's Food Surplus Into the Charitable Food System. One of the study recommendations to increase charitable food system sourcing highlights, "Increase investment in CFS farm surplus purchasing programs (e.g. Mainers Feeding Mainers) to support farms, minimize food loss, and stock regional Maine food banks."
Finally, our team partnered with the MDEP to lead our state's recent Materials Management Task Force (2024), comprised of key stakeholders in Maine's waste management systems (business, state, municipal, and community representatives). The task force was tasked with making recommendations to improve the economic, social and environmental outcomes of Maine's waste management system. Our wasted food and food loss subgroup developed three key recommendations including, "Maximize food rescue, recovery and donation of edible food through state tax credits, clearer liability protections, support for donation infrastructure, and preventing organizational policies that mandate disposal of edible food. "
Based on our recent Maine statewide, community-engaged, stakeholder-led research, we believe that LD415 which requests an additional $1M per year of state investment in the Mainers Feeding Mainers program which would support the harvesting, processing, and transport of good, edible, nutritious Maine farm food that might otherwise go uneaten is exactly the type of win-win-win initiative that should be funded.
My colleagues and I would be happy to provide any additional information or answer any questions. Thank you for your strong support of the University of Maine which makes our research possible.
Susanne Lee Faculty Fellow Sen. George J. Mitchell Center for Sustainability Solutions University of Maine
